    AI Overview
    Spring is the temperate season between winter and summer, characterized by warming temperatures, blooming plants, and longer days. In 2026, the Northern Hemisphere spring officially begins with the vernal equinox on March 20, bringing renewed growth and animal activity. It typically spans March-May (North) or September-November (South). 
    Key Characteristics and Timing 
    • Start Date: The 2026 spring equinox occurs on March 20 at 10:46 a.m. EDT, marking the moment the sun crosses the equator.
    • Months: Generally, spring includes March, April, and May in the Northern Hemisphere, while it is September, October, and November in the Southern Hemisphere
      .
    • Characteristics: This season is marked by rising temperatures, melting snow, and increasing daylight as the hemisphere tilts toward the sun.
    • Meteorological Definition: Meteorologists often define spring as lasting from March 1 to May 31. 
    Effects on Nature 
    • Plant Life: Warmer weather and increased sunlight trigger the budding of trees, the germination of seeds, and the blooming of flowers.
    • Animal Life: Animals often emerge from hibernation, migrate back to warmer climates, and begin breeding or nesting activities, with increased food availability. 
    What is the Vernal Equinox?
    The vernal equinox is the moment when the center of the sun crosses Earth's equator, resulting in nearly equal lengths of day and night across the planet. It is considered the astronomical start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere.

    Is March 20 the first day of spring?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    No, the first day of spring is not always on March 20
    . While it often falls on that date, the astronomical vernal equinox can occur on March 19, 20, or 21. This variation is caused by slight wobbles in the Earth's axis and the difference between the Gregorian calendar (365 days) and the solar year (about 365.24 days). 
    • Most Common: Between 1980 and 2102, the equinox will be on March 19 or 20, with 21 becoming rare, according to Space.com.
    • 2026 Timing: The first day of spring in 2026 is Friday, March 20, at 10:46 a.m. EDT, says the Cincinnati Enquirer.
    • Alternative Definition: Some people also recognize "meteorological spring," which always begins on March 1st, according to
      a post on Facebook from the Met Office.
       
    The equinox marks the precise moment the sun crosses the Earth's equator, bringing roughly equal day and night across the globe, as mentioned in this article on weather.com.

      Impact on Plants. How does the spring season affect plant life?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Spring triggers plant life to awaken and grow through warmer temperatures, increased sunlight, and moisture, activating processes like germination, budding, and flowering, as plants use these cues to photosynthesize, produce leaves, and prepare for reproduction, kickstarting the annual growth cycle after winter dormancy.
       
      Key Effects of Spring on Plants:
      • Warmth & Soil: Rising soil temperatures and increased moisture from rain (or melting snow) signal roots to become active, absorbing water and nutrients, while warmer air promotes germination for seeds and growth for perennials. 
      • Longer Days & Sunlight: Longer daylight hours increase photosynthesis, giving plants the energy to produce more leaves and flowers, which is crucial for biomass and food production. 
      • Hormonal Triggers: Increased light and warmth activate dormant genes, leading to the production of hormones like florigen, which directs energy towards budding and blooming. 
      • Bud Burst & Leafing Out: Plants expend stored energy to push out new leaves and flowers, a vulnerable process susceptible to late frosts, as water in new tissues can freeze. 
      • Reproduction: For many plants, spring is the primary time to flower and disperse pollen, completing their life cycle. 
      • Phenology & Climate Change: Earlier springs due to warming temperatures are shifting plant development (phenology) earlier, impacting ecosystems and agriculture, sometimes leading to water stress later in the year. 
      In essence, spring is the vital transition from dormancy to active growth, driven by environmental cues that signal it's safe and energy-rich to grow, flower, and reproduce.

        Key Characteristics. What are the key characteristics of the spring season?
        About this result

        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        Spring's key characteristics are renewal and growth, marked by warmer, longer days, melting snow, blooming flowers, sprouting leaves, and the return of migratory animals, signifying the transition from winter's cold to summer's warmth, driven by the Earth tilting towards the sun.
         
        Ecological Changes
        • Plant Life: Dormant plants awaken, trees bud and grow new leaves, and flowers like daffodils, tulips, and bluebells bloom, often with fragrant scents. 
        • Animal Activity: Migratory birds return, hibernating animals emerge, and insects like bees become active, pollinating plants. 
        • Weather: Temperatures rise, snow melts (swelling streams), and rainfall often increases, creating ideal conditions for growth. 
        Astronomical & Daylight
        • Longer Days: The vernal equinox marks the start of days becoming longer and nights shorter as the Earth tilts towards the sun. 
        • Sunlight: Increased sunshine boosts moods and provides energy for growth. 
        Atmosphere & Feeling
        • Renewal & Rebirth: A strong sense of new beginnings, hope, and life returning after winter. 
        • Mild Temperatures: A comfortable "Goldilocks zone" between winter's chill and summer's heat. 
        Cultural Significance
        • Symbolism: Universally represents rebirth, joy, and fertility in art, religion, and festivals like Easter, Holi, and Earth Day.

          Celebrations. What are the cultural or religious celebrations during the spring season?
          About this result

          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          Spring is filled with cultural and religious celebrations marking renewal, like Easter (Christianity), Passover (Judaism), and Holi (Hinduism), alongside secular traditions such as Nowruz (Persian New Year) and Songkran (Thai New Year), all celebrating themes of rebirth, light, and new beginnings through unique festivals, rituals, and feasts worldwide. 
          Religious Celebrations
          • Christianity: Easter (Resurrection of Jesus), Lent (period of fasting and reflection leading to Easter). 
          • Judaism: Passover (liberation from Egypt), Shavuot (harvest festival). 
          • Hinduism: Holi (festival of colors, victory of good over evil). 
          • Sikhism: Vaisakhi (harvest festival, founding of the Khalsa). 
          • Islam: Ramadan (month of fasting and prayer), Eid al-Fitr (end of Ramadan) and Eid al-Adha (Feast of Sacrifice) often fall in spring depending on the lunar calendar. 
          Cultural & Secular Celebrations
          • Nowruz: Persian New Year, celebrated on the Spring Equinox with spring cleaning, bonfires, and family gatherings.
          • Songkran: Thai New Year, marked by water fights and purification rituals. 
          • Hanami: Japanese tradition of cherry blossom viewing, involving picnics under blooming trees. 
          • Spring Equinox Festivals: Observances at ancient sites like Teotihuacán (Mexico) and Stonehenge (UK) to welcome the sun and fertility. 
          • White House Easter Egg Roll: A popular American tradition symbolizing spring fun. 
          Common Themes
          • Rebirth & Renewal: Symbolized by new growth, resurrection, and the return of warmth. 
          • Light & Good over Evil: Celebrated through bonfires (Nowruz, Holi) and the emergence from darkness (Easter). 
          • Harvest & Fertility: Honoring agricultural cycles with feasts and rituals.
